title: PostgreSQL With Raw SQL
summary: See what an ORM does and why this course skips it, then connect with psycopg, run migrations, and write safe parameterized queries.
intro: Roombook's repository still keeps its bookings in a list, and the previous lesson designed the tables that will replace it. This lesson connects the two. It starts with a choice every project makes: most frameworks offer an ORM, a library that writes your SQL for you, and this course writes its own SQL with psycopg instead, for reasons part 1 explains. Then it opens a pool of database connections, creates the tables with migrations, reads rows without letting anyone inject SQL, writes rows, and turns the database's errors into API errors. By the end, the in-memory repository is gone, and the service never noticed.

steps.title: ORMs, and why this course writes SQL
steps.body:
Every FastAPI project decides how its code talks to the database, and the choice shapes the rest of the code. The popular answer is an ORM. This course takes the other road and writes its SQL by hand. This part explains what an ORM does, what it costs, and why learning SQL first is the better start.

## What an ORM does

An **ORM**, an object-relational mapper, maps your classes to tables and your objects to rows. You describe a Booking class once, and the ORM writes the SQL. Saving a new object becomes an INSERT, changing a field and saving becomes an UPDATE, and a call like `session.scalars(select(Booking).where(Booking.user_id == user_id))`, from SQLAlchemy, the ORM most Python projects use, becomes a SELECT. Many ORMs also create the tables from your classes.

That's appealing. Simple endpoints need very little code, the types come for free, and you rarely write SQL at all.

## What it costs

- **You can't see the queries.** The SQL is made at run time, out of sight. A harmless-looking line can send a query that reads a whole table, and you find out when the endpoint is slow.
- **The N+1 problem.** You met N+1 with GraphQL's resolvers, and ORMs cause it the same way. Most load related rows lazily, the first time your code touches them. List 50 bookings and show each one's room name, and the ORM sends one query for the bookings, then one more for each booking's room: 51 queries where one JOIN would do. It's the most common reason ORM code is slow.
- **It's a second language.** Each ORM has its own way to write filters, joins, and groups, and whatever it can't express falls back to SQL. So you end up needing both.
- **It hides what the database can do.** The rules that keep Roombook correct, like refusing two bookings that overlap, are database features most ORMs can't describe. Teams on an ORM often skip them, and the rule moves into code that a second writer can get around.

## The spectrum

Database libraries fall along a line, from writing every query yourself to never seeing one:

```diagram raw-sql-spectrum
From writing every query yourself to never seeing one.
```

- A **driver** sends the SQL you write and hands back the rows. This course uses psycopg.
- A **query builder** builds SQL from function calls, which helps when a query changes shape at run time.
- **SQL-first** tools read SQL you write in files and give you typed functions that run it.
- An **ORM** maps classes to tables and writes the SQL itself.

| Step | Libraries for Python |
|---|---|
| Driver | psycopg, asyncpg |
| Query builder | SQLAlchemy Core |
| SQL-first | aiosql, which turns named queries in `.sql` files into functions |
| ORM | SQLAlchemy's ORM, SQLModel, Tortoise ORM, Django's ORM |

SQLAlchemy is two libraries in one: Core is a query builder, and the ORM sits on top. This course skips both so the SQL stays in plain sight.

## Why this course writes SQL

You'll learn what the database really does, and every query Roombook sends sits in its repository, where you can read it, check it with EXPLAIN, and fix it. SQL also lasts. It's the same in every language and framework, so what you learn here carries over to your next project, while an ORM's API doesn't. And picking up an ORM once you know SQL is easy, because you can see through it. Going the other way is hard.

None of that makes ORMs wrong. Plenty of teams ship good software with one, especially apps that are mostly forms over tables. When you meet one, you'll know what it does underneath, and that's when it helps most.

steps.title: Connecting through a pool
steps.body:
Every request that reads or writes data needs a connection to the database, and the way you manage connections decides how many requests the API can serve at once. Opening a new one for each request is the classic first mistake. This part explains what a connection costs, how a pool fixes it, and how Roombook opens one at startup and closes it at shutdown.

## What a connection costs

A connection is a long-lived conversation between your API and the database server. Opening one takes several steps: a TCP connection, often a TLS handshake for encryption, then logging in with a user name and password. PostgreSQL then starts a new process on the server just for that connection, which costs time and several megabytes of memory. Altogether that's a few milliseconds before the first query can run, often longer than the query itself.

The server also limits how many connections it accepts at once, 100 by default, a setting called `max_connections`. An API that opens one per request hits that limit under load, and the requests past it fail.

## A pool

A **connection pool** opens a few connections and keeps them open. When a request needs the database, it **borrows** a connection, runs its queries, and **returns** it, so the next request can use it. Borrowing an open connection takes microseconds.

```diagram raw-sql-pool
Four requests share three open connections. The fourth waits for one to come back.
```

In the diagram, three requests each hold a connection, and the fourth waits. If no connection comes back in time, the pool gives up with a timeout error, which the API answers with a 503. That limit is a feature: it keeps a burst of traffic from flooding the database.

A small pool is usually right. PostgreSQL works on only as many queries at once as its server has CPU cores, so a pool of 100 just moves the queue from your API into the database, where waiting costs more. Ten connections for each copy of the API is a good start. Each copy has its own pool, so the copies times the pool size must stay under `max_connections`. The lesson on databases at scale comes back to that.

## The connection URL

The pool needs to know where the database is and how to log in. That's the connection URL from psql in the previous lesson. It comes from the environment, never from the code, because it holds a password and differs on every computer:

```env
DATABASE_URL=postgres://roombook:roombook@localhost:5432/roombook
```

That line goes in your `.env` file, which stays out of git. `get_settings()`, from `app/config.py`, reads it into `settings.database_url`, the same way it read the middleware lesson's settings. In production, the platform sets `DATABASE_URL` for you.

## Open at startup, close at shutdown

First add the driver and its pool to the project with `uv add "psycopg[binary,pool]"`. The `pool` extra brings `psycopg_pool`, and `binary` brings psycopg's compiled part ready-made, so nothing has to be built on your computer.

Make one pool when the app starts, and close it when the app stops. FastAPI runs code at those two moments through a **lifespan**: a function you pass as `FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)`, where the code before its `yield` runs at startup, before the first request, and the code after it runs at shutdown, after the last one:

```python
from psycopg_pool import AsyncConnectionPool


def create_pool(database_url: str) -> AsyncConnectionPool:
    return AsyncConnectionPool(
        conninfo=database_url,
        min_size=1,
        max_size=10,
        timeout=5.0,
        kwargs={"autocommit": True},
        open=False,
    )
```

```python sketch
@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI) -> AsyncIterator[None]:
    settings = get_settings()
    pool = create_pool(settings.database_url)
    await pool.open(wait=True)
    app.state.pool = pool
    yield
    await pool.close()
```

`min_size` and `max_size` bound the pool. `timeout` is how many seconds a request waits to borrow a connection before psycopg raises `PoolTimeout`. `open=False` keeps the pool closed until the lifespan opens it, and `wait=True` makes startup fail at once if the database can't be reached. `autocommit=True` makes each statement take effect the moment it runs, which is what most drivers do by default. Without it, psycopg starts a transaction on every connection and waits for you to commit, and a forgotten commit quietly loses your writes. The next lesson starts transactions on purpose when it needs them.

A dependency borrows one connection for each request and gives it back when the request ends. It's a `yield` dependency, the kind the MVC lesson mentioned: FastAPI runs it up to the `yield` before the endpoint, hands the endpoint what it yielded, and runs the rest once the request is done, here the end of the `async with`, which returns the connection to the pool. The service is built on that connection:

```python sketch
async def get_conn(request: Request) -> AsyncIterator[AsyncConnection]:
    async with request.app.state.pool.connection() as conn:
        yield conn


Conn = Annotated[AsyncConnection, Depends(get_conn)]


def get_booking_service(request: Request, conn: Conn) -> BookingService:
    return BookingService(PgBookingRepository(conn), PgRoomRepository(conn), request.app.state.clock)
```

FastAPI runs a dependency once per request, so every repository in one request shares that one connection. This is the move the MVC lesson promised. The service is no longer built once in `create_app` and kept on `app.state`: `get_booking_service` builds a fresh one for each request, around that request's connection, and `app.state` keeps only what lives as long as the app, like the pool and the clock. `get_room_repository` changes the same way, to `PgRoomRepository(conn)`. The endpoints still ask for `service: BookingServiceDep`, so none of them changes.

steps.title: Migrations in plain SQL
steps.body:
Your tables have to exist before the API can use them, and they'll change as Roombook grows: a new column, a new index, a new table. Every copy of the database, on your computer, on a teammate's, in the tests, and in production, needs exactly the same changes in the same order. Typing CREATE TABLE into psql on each one can't keep up. Migrations do.

## What a migration is

A **migration** is a file of SQL that changes the schema by one step, with a number in its name that sets its place in line. A **migration runner** keeps a table in the database that records which files have run. Each time, it applies the files that aren't in that table yet, in order, each inside a **transaction**, a group of statements that takes effect completely or not at all, and records them. So a fresh database gets every file, and one that's up to date gets none.

PostgreSQL can undo a CREATE TABLE or an ALTER TABLE that fails halfway, which many databases can't. So a migration that fails leaves nothing behind, and you can fix the file and run it again.

## The rules

- **Never edit a migration that has run anywhere but your own computer.** Other databases already applied the old version and won't run it again, so your change would reach some databases and not others. Fix it forward with a new migration.
- **One change per file, named for what it does**: `004_create_bookings.sql`, `005_add_bookings_no_overlap.sql`.
- **Keep data out of them, mostly.** Data to try things with, like Ada and the Turing room, goes in a separate seed script. A migration moves data only when the schema change needs it.
- **Make each change safe for the code that's already running.** While a new version rolls out, old copies of the API still run against the new schema. Adding a column is safe. Renaming one breaks the old code, so you add the new column, copy the data, switch the code over, and drop the old column in a later release.

## Roombook's first migrations

Roombook starts with four files, one per table, in the order the foreign keys need them: `migrations/001_create_buildings.sql`, `002_create_users.sql`, `003_create_rooms.sql`, and `004_create_bookings.sql`. Buildings come first, since rooms point at them, and bookings last. Here's `migrations/004_create_bookings.sql`:

```sql
CREATE TABLE bookings (
  id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY (START WITH 1001) PRIMARY KEY,
  room_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES rooms (id),
  user_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES users (id),
  starts_at timestamptz NOT NULL,
  ends_at timestamptz NOT NULL,
  attendees integer NOT NULL CHECK (attendees > 0),
  note text,
  status text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'confirmed'
    CHECK (status IN ('confirmed', 'cancelled')),
  version integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  cancelled_at timestamptz,
  CHECK (ends_at > starts_at)
);

CREATE INDEX bookings_user_starts_idx ON bookings (user_id, starts_at);
CREATE INDEX bookings_room_starts_idx ON bookings (room_id, starts_at);
```

The other three files hold the CREATE TABLE statements from the data modeling lesson, with the CHECK rules, the foreign keys, and the unique index on `lower(email)` there from the start. The next lesson explains those rules, along with the one against overlapping bookings, which arrives in the fifth migration.

## The runner: a short script

Roombook needs very little from a migration tool, so a script of about thirty lines does the job: `scripts/migrate.py`, which the next example shows. It keeps its record in a table called `schema_migrations`, with one row per file that has run. It takes a lock first, `pg_advisory_lock`, a lock PostgreSQL holds under a number you choose, so that two servers starting at once don't both run the same file. Then it runs each new file inside `conn.transaction()`, which commits when the block ends, or rolls back if anything inside it fails, so a file either applies completely or not at all. A script that runs once has no need for async code or a pool, so it uses psycopg's plain synchronous `connect`.

Run it with `uv run scripts/migrate.py` before you start the server, and as a step of every release, which the deploy lesson sets up. The script reads `DATABASE_URL` straight from the environment, not through `get_settings()`, so either set the variable in your terminal first or add `--env-file .env` to `uv run`, which loads your `.env` file for the command. The same goes for the small scripts later in this lesson. Alembic is the tool most Python projects use, but it's built around SQLAlchemy, which this course skips.

examples.title: The migration script, and its first run
examples.prompt: `scripts/migrate.py`, run with `uv run scripts/migrate.py` against an empty database.
examples.code:
import os
from pathlib import Path

import psycopg

MIGRATIONS = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "migrations"


def main() -> None:
    with psycopg.connect(os.environ["DATABASE_URL"], autocommit=True) as conn:
        conn.execute("""
            CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS schema_migrations (
              name text PRIMARY KEY,
              applied_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
            )""")
        # One runner at a time, even if two servers start together.
        conn.execute("SELECT pg_advisory_lock(7310)")

        rows = conn.execute("SELECT name FROM schema_migrations").fetchall()
        applied = {name for (name,) in rows}

        for path in sorted(MIGRATIONS.glob("*.sql")):
            if path.name in applied:
                continue
            with conn.transaction():
                conn.execute(path.read_bytes())
                conn.execute(
                    "INSERT INTO schema_migrations (name) VALUES (%s)", (path.name,)
                )
            print(f"applied {path.name}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
examples.explanation: The script prints each file it applies. Running it again prints nothing, since every file is already in `schema_migrations`. If a file fails, `conn.transaction()` rolls it back completely, the error stops the script, and the files before it stay applied, so you fix the file and run the script again. `sorted()` puts the files in name order, which is why the names start with zero-padded numbers: `010` sorts after `009`, while `10` would sort before `9`. It passes the file's bytes, `read_bytes()`, because psycopg's type hints accept SQL text only when it's written in your code. That's the same check that guards against injection in part 4.

steps.title: Parameters, not string building
steps.body:
The best-known security hole in web apps comes from one habit: building a query by pasting a user's input into the SQL text. This part shows the attack, the one fix that always works, and then how a row from the database becomes one of your own types.

## SQL injection

Say the login endpoint finds a user by email, and builds the query by joining strings:

```python sketch
# Never do this.
cur = await conn.execute(f"SELECT id, email, role FROM users WHERE email = '{email}'")
```

With `ada@roombook.example`, it sends the query it meant to. Now someone types `' OR '1'='1` as the email. The first quote closes the string early, and the rest becomes SQL: `WHERE email = '' OR '1'='1'`, which is true for every row, so the query returns every user. With a little more typing, an attacker can read other tables, or change and delete data. That's **SQL injection**, and it's been near the top of every list of web attacks for twenty years. The security lesson comes back to it.

## Parameters

The fix is to never put a value into the SQL text. You write a **placeholder** where each value goes, and pass the values separately:

```python sketch
cur = await conn.execute("SELECT id, email, role FROM users WHERE email = %s", (email,))
```

psycopg's placeholder is `%s` for every type, or `%(name)s` with a dict of values. It looks like Python's old `%` formatting, but it isn't: psycopg turns each one into PostgreSQL's own `$1`, `$2`, and sends the values apart. So never format the string yourself, with `%` or an f-string. psycopg's type hints help here, since `execute` only accepts SQL text that's written out in your code, and a type checker flags an f-string. From Python 3.14, psycopg also accepts a **template string**, written `t"... {email}"`. Unlike an f-string, a template string keeps each value apart from the text, and psycopg sends it as a parameter. One letter separates the safe version from the dangerous one, so read them closely.

```diagram raw-sql-injection
Pasted into the text, input becomes SQL. Sent as a parameter, it stays data.
```

The driver sends the SQL text and the values to PostgreSQL as separate parts of one message. PostgreSQL works out what the SQL means first, and only then fills in the values, as plain data. A value can hold quotes, semicolons, or the word DROP, and it's still just text to compare with an email. Nothing is escaped, so there's nothing to escape from.

Joining pieces of SQL that you wrote in the code is fine, and part 5 does it to add filters. The rule is that a value from outside the code, from a request, a file, or even your own database, never becomes part of the SQL text. Placeholders only hold values, though. A table name, a column name, or a word like DESC can't be a parameter, so when the request picks one, like a sort order, you choose it from a fixed list in your code. Part 5 shows how.

## From a row to your type

psycopg turns PostgreSQL's types into Python's: `text` into `str`, `integer` and `bigint` into `int`, since Python's integers have no size limit, `boolean` into `bool`, `timestamptz` into a `datetime` with its time zone set, `numeric` into `Decimal`, arrays into lists, and NULL into `None`.

Each row comes back as a tuple unless you pick a **row factory**. `class_row(Booking)` calls `Booking(**columns)` for every row, so each column's name must match a field of the `Booking` dataclass from the MVC lesson. Python names are snake_case too, so `starts_at` lands on `starts_at` with no mapping at all, and the camelCase names in the JSON come from the response schema's aliases, as in the request data lesson. The repository holds the connection it was given:

```python
class PgBookingRepository:
    def __init__(self, conn: AsyncConnection) -> None:
        self._conn = conn

    async def get(self, booking_id: int) -> Booking | None:
        async with self._conn.cursor(row_factory=class_row(Booking)) as cur:
            await cur.execute(
                """
                SELECT id, room_id, user_id, starts_at, ends_at,
                       attendees, note, status, version, created_at
                FROM bookings
                WHERE id = %s
                """,
                (booking_id,),
            )
            return await cur.fetchone()
```

Times come back in the connection's time zone, which is UTC in the `postgres:18` image. Whatever the zone, it's the same instant, and the response schema writes it in UTC with a `Z`.

## One row, or none

`fetchone()` returns `None` when no row matched, so `get` returns `None`, and the service raises the not-found problem from the validation lesson, a 404. A missing row is a normal answer, not an error. Errors are for queries that fail.

examples.title: An injection, and the same input as a parameter
examples.prompt: The first file shows the two queries the string-building code sends. The second runs the same lookup with a real parameter, in psql, using PREPARE, which names a statement with a placeholder, and EXECUTE, which runs it with a value.
examples.output:
id |        email         |  role
----+----------------------+--------
  1 | ada@roombook.example | member
(1 row)

 id |         email          |  role
----+------------------------+--------
  1 | ada@roombook.example   | member
  2 | grace@roombook.example | staff
  3 | alan@roombook.example  | admin
(3 rows)

PREPARE

 id |        email         |  role
----+----------------------+--------
  1 | ada@roombook.example | member
(1 row)

 id | email | role
----+-------+------
(0 rows)
examples.explanation: The first query finds Ada. The second is what the email `' OR '1'='1` turned the code's query into, and it returns all three users, Alan the admin included, without anyone knowing a password. The prepared version takes the same input as a value for `$1`. To write it in SQL, each quote inside the value is doubled, but PostgreSQL then sees one value: the text `' OR '1'='1`. No user has that email, so it finds none. That's exactly what the driver does for you on every query, with no doubling needed, since the values never mix with the text.

examples.title: Reading a booking through the repository
examples.prompt: A quick script, `scripts/try_repository.py`, that borrows a connection and asks the repository for booking 1001, then for booking 99, which doesn't exist. Run it with `uv run python -m scripts.try_repository`.
examples.code:
import asyncio
import os

from app.bookings.repository import PgBookingRepository
from app.db import create_pool


async def main() -> None:
    async with create_pool(os.environ["DATABASE_URL"]) as pool:
        async with pool.connection() as conn:
            bookings = PgBookingRepository(conn)
            print(await bookings.get(1001))
            print(await bookings.get(99))


asyncio.run(main())
examples.output:
Booking(id=1001, room_id=1, user_id=1, starts_at=datetime.datetime(2026, 10, 5, 14, 0, tzinfo=datetime.timezone.utc), ends_at=datetime.datetime(2026, 10, 5, 15, 30, tzinfo=datetime.timezone.utc), attendees=3, note='Algorithms study group', status='confirmed', version=1, created_at=datetime.datetime(2026, 10, 1, 9, 0, tzinfo=datetime.timezone.utc))
None
examples.explanation: The first line is the `Booking` dataclass, built by `class_row` from one row. The ids and attendees are plain `int`s, the note is a `str`, and the three times are `datetime` objects with `tzinfo` set to UTC, so they're exact instants, safe to compare with the service's clock. Booking 99 doesn't exist, so `fetchone()` found nothing and `get` returned `None`. `async with create_pool(...)` opens the pool and closes it at the end, like the lifespan does for the app, and `-m` runs the script as a module, so `from app...` imports work from the project's folder.

steps.title: Lists: filters, pages, and N+1
steps.body:
A list endpoint like `GET /v1/bookings?status=confirmed&from=2026-10-01` is where queries get interesting. Its filters are optional, so the SQL changes shape from one request to the next. The list comes back a page at a time. And each booking may need data from another table. This part builds the repository method behind it.

## Optional filters

Each filter the request sends adds one condition to the WHERE, with its value as a parameter. Building the WHERE from fixed pieces of SQL written in your code is safe. What varies is which pieces you use, and every value still travels as a parameter.

```python sketch
async def list_for_user(self, q: BookingQuery) -> list[Booking]:
    where = [sql.SQL("user_id = %s")]
    params: list[object] = [q.user_id]
    if q.status is not None:
        where.append(sql.SQL("status = %s"))
        params.append(q.status)
    if q.starts_from is not None:
        where.append(sql.SQL("starts_at >= %s"))
        params.append(q.starts_from)
    if q.starts_before is not None:
        where.append(sql.SQL("starts_at < %s"))
        params.append(q.starts_before)
    if q.after is not None:
        where.append(sql.SQL("(starts_at, id) > (%s, %s)"))
        params.extend(q.after)
    params.append(q.limit + 1)
    query = sql.SQL("""
        SELECT id, room_id, user_id, starts_at, ends_at,
               attendees, note, status, version, created_at
        FROM bookings
        WHERE {where}
        ORDER BY starts_at, id
        LIMIT %s
        """).format(where=sql.SQL(" AND ").join(where))
    async with self._conn.cursor(row_factory=class_row(Booking)) as cur:
        await cur.execute(query, params)
        return await cur.fetchall()
```

`psycopg.sql` builds SQL from pieces safely. `sql.SQL` marks text written in your code as SQL, `join` glues pieces with ` AND `, and `format` fills the `{where}` slot with other `sql` pieces, never with values. The values stay behind `%s` placeholders, in `params`, in the same order.

## Pages with a cursor

The request data lesson chose **keyset pagination**, also called cursor pagination: each page starts right after the last row of the page before, found by the sort's columns. Roombook sorts bookings by `(starts_at, id)`. The id breaks ties, since two bookings can start at the same moment, and without it a page could skip one or show it twice. The condition `(starts_at, id) > (...)` compares the pair in order: a later start, or the same start with a higher id. With the `(user_id, starts_at)` index, PostgreSQL jumps straight to that spot, so page 500 is as fast as page 1. An `OFFSET 10000` would read and throw away ten thousand rows first.

The method asks for one row more than the page holds. If that extra row comes back, there's another page: the service drops it, and builds `nextCursor` from the last row it keeps. If not, `nextCursor` is null.

## Sorting from an allowlist

A placeholder can't hold a column name, so a `sort` parameter needs another approach. Map each value the API accepts to a fixed piece of SQL, and refuse anything else with a 422:

```python sketch
ROOM_SORTS = {
    "name": sql.SQL("name, id"),
    "capacity": sql.SQL("capacity, id"),
}

# sort was checked against these keys by the query schema.
query = sql.SQL(
    "SELECT id, building_id, name, capacity FROM rooms ORDER BY {order} LIMIT %s"
).format(order=ROOM_SORTS[sort])
```

When you need a single name from a list, `sql.Identifier("capacity")` writes it as a quoted name, which is safe even for odd names.

The request picks a key, and the SQL comes only from your code.

## N+1, and how to avoid it

Say the bookings list shows each room's name. Fetching each booking's room one at a time is the N+1 pattern from part 1, and it's just as slow without an ORM. There are two fixes:

- **JOIN** the rooms in the same query, when you always need them together.
- **Fetch them all at once.** Collect the room ids from the page, and ask for all of them in one query with `WHERE id = ANY($1)`. psycopg turns a Python list into a PostgreSQL array:

```python sketch
async def room_names(self, room_ids: list[int]) -> dict[int, str]:
    cur = await self._conn.execute(
        "SELECT id, name FROM rooms WHERE id = ANY(%s)", (room_ids,)
    )
    return {room_id: name for room_id, name in await cur.fetchall()}
```

Either way, it's at most two queries, however long the page.

examples.title: Two pages of Ada's bookings
examples.prompt: Ada has five bookings in the seed data, a different set from the ones earlier lessons made in memory, and a page holds two. Ask for three rows to learn whether there's a next page, then ask for the page after the last row shown.
examples.code:
-- Page 1: two bookings, plus one more to learn if a next page exists.
SELECT id, room_id, starts_at
FROM bookings
WHERE user_id = 1
ORDER BY starts_at, id
LIMIT 3;

-- Page 2: the rows after the last one shown, (2026-10-06 10:00, id 1002).
SELECT id, room_id, starts_at
FROM bookings
WHERE user_id = 1
  AND (starts_at, id) > ('2026-10-06 10:00Z', 1002)
ORDER BY starts_at, id
LIMIT 3;
examples.explanation: The first query returns three rows, one more than a page, so there's a next page. The API sends bookings 1001 and 1002, and builds the cursor from booking 1002: its start, 6 October at 10:00, and its id. The second query starts right after that pair and again gets three rows, so it sends 1004 and 1005, and there's a page after it too. Bookings 1005 and 1006 start at exactly the same moment, and only the id decides their order. Without it, the cut between two pages could fall between them and lose one. Booking 1003 never shows up, since it's Grace's.

steps.title: Writing rows and reading errors
steps.body:
Writes are where the API changes data, and where the database's rules push back. This part covers INSERT for POST, UPDATE for PUT and PATCH, telling whether a write found its row, and turning the database's refusals into the API errors from the validation lesson. It ends with the swap this lesson has been building up to.

## INSERT ... RETURNING

A new booking gets its id, status, version, and timestamps from the table's defaults. **RETURNING** lists columns to send back from the rows a statement wrote, so one round trip saves the booking and returns it, ready for the 201 response:

```python sketch
async def insert(self, b: NewBooking) -> Booking:
    try:
        async with self._conn.cursor(row_factory=class_row(Booking)) as cur:
            await cur.execute(
                """
                INSERT INTO bookings
                  (room_id, user_id, starts_at, ends_at, attendees, note)
                VALUES (%s, %s, %s, %s, %s, %s)
                RETURNING id, room_id, user_id, starts_at, ends_at,
                          attendees, note, status, version, created_at
                """,
                (b.room_id, b.user_id, b.starts_at, b.ends_at, b.attendees, b.note),
            )
            row = await cur.fetchone()
    except errors.ForeignKeyViolation as e:
        raise UnprocessableError("room-not-found", "That room doesn't exist.") from e
    except errors.ExclusionViolation as e:
        raise ConflictError("booking-overlap", "The room is already booked then.") from e
    assert row is not None
    return row
```

## UPDATE for PUT and PATCH

A PUT replaces the whole resource, so its UPDATE sets every column the client may change. A PATCH sets only the fields the request sent, which means building the SET list the way part 5 built the WHERE. The request data lesson drew the line between a missing field, which means leave it alone, and a null one, which means clear it. In Pydantic, `model_dump(exclude_unset=True)` gives only the fields the request sent, with `None` for the ones it set to null, so the repository adds `note = %s` only for keys in that dict. Both kinds add one to `version`, which the next lesson uses to catch two people editing the same booking at once.

## Did it find the row?

An UPDATE or a DELETE that matches no rows isn't an error to the database. It reports `UPDATE 0` and moves on, so the repository has to check the count. psycopg reports the count as the cursor's `rowcount`. Cancelling uses it: `WHERE id = ... AND status = 'confirmed'` changes one row the first time and none the second, so the method returns whether it did anything, and the service decides on the answer.

```python sketch
async def cancel(self, booking_id: int) -> bool:
    cur = await self._conn.execute(
        """
        UPDATE bookings
        SET status = 'cancelled', cancelled_at = now(), updated_at = now()
        WHERE id = %s AND status = 'confirmed'
        """,
        (booking_id,),
    )
    return cur.rowcount == 1
```

Deleting a room in Roombook is a soft delete, `UPDATE rooms SET active = false`, so its old bookings still point at a real row. A real `DELETE FROM` is for rows nothing points at.

## When the database says no

Every PostgreSQL error carries a **SQLSTATE**, a five-character code that names the problem the same way in every driver and every language. The ones an API meets most start with 23, the class for broken rules:

| SQLSTATE | Name | Roombook example | Answer |
|---|---|---|---|
| `23505` | unique_violation | a second account for one email | 409 |
| `23503` | foreign_key_violation | a booking for room 99, which doesn't exist | 422 |
| `23514` | check_violation | a room with a capacity of 50 | 422 |
| `23P01` | exclusion_violation | two bookings that overlap, from the next lesson | 409 |
| `23502` | not_null_violation | a value the code forgot to send | 500, a bug |

Validation at the edge should catch bad values before they get this far, so a 23514 usually means a check is missing from the schema. A 23505 or a 23P01 is different: only the database can see all the other rows, so those errors are the normal way to learn about a conflict. The error also names the rule that failed, like `bookings_room_id_fkey`, so one SQLSTATE can lead to different answers depending on the rule.

psycopg raises a different exception class for each SQLSTATE, all in `psycopg.errors`: `UniqueViolation`, `ForeignKeyViolation`, `CheckViolation`, and `ExclusionViolation`. So `insert` catches the ones it expects and raises the domain's errors, with `from e` keeping the original attached for the logs. Each exception also has `e.sqlstate`, and `e.diag.constraint_name` names the rule, for when one SQLSTATE needs different answers.

The repository turns the errors it expects into domain errors, so nothing above it knows about the driver. Anything else goes up unchanged, and the central error handler answers 500 and logs the details.

## The swap

That's the whole repository, and `PgRoomRepository` does the same for rooms. `get_booking_service`, from part 2, builds the service on them in place of the in-memory repositories from the MVC lesson, and that's the only place that changes. The service still awaits `get`, `insert`, and `count_upcoming`, now with `cancel` and `list_for_user` beside them, and gets the same `Booking` back, so it never learns that the data now lives in PostgreSQL. The in-memory version moves to the tests, in `tests/fakes.py`, where the testing lesson uses it to check the service without a database.

The bookings now live in PostgreSQL, but nothing in the database stops two of them from overlapping yet. The next lesson adds the rules that do, and the transactions that make several changes happen together.

examples.title: Writing, and getting the result back
examples.prompt: With only the three bookings from the data modeling lesson stored, create a booking, change its attendees and clear its note in one UPDATE, then try to cancel booking 99.
examples.explanation: The INSERT gave the new booking the next id, 1004, and filled `status` and `version` from their defaults, and RETURNING sent them back with no second query. The UPDATE set two columns and bumped `version` to 2. Its note is NULL now, which psql prints as an empty space. The last UPDATE matched nothing, since there's no booking 99, so it reports `UPDATE 0` rather than an error, and the repository's count check is what turns that into a 404. `updated_at = now()` keeps the time of the last change, and the next lesson moves that job into the database.

examples.title: What a broken rule looks like in psycopg
examples.prompt: A quick script, `scripts/try_fk.py`, that tries to book room 99 and prints what the exception carries. Run it with `uv run python -m scripts.try_fk`.
examples.code:
import asyncio
import os
from datetime import UTC, datetime

from psycopg import errors

from app.db import create_pool


async def main() -> None:
    async with create_pool(os.environ["DATABASE_URL"]) as pool:
        async with pool.connection() as conn:
            try:
                await conn.execute(
                    """
                    INSERT INTO bookings (room_id, user_id, starts_at, ends_at, attendees)
                    VALUES (%s, %s, %s, %s, %s)
                    """,
                    (99, 1, datetime(2026, 10, 7, 9, tzinfo=UTC),
                     datetime(2026, 10, 7, 10, tzinfo=UTC), 2),
                )
            except errors.ForeignKeyViolation as e:
                print(type(e).__name__, e.sqlstate, e.diag.constraint_name)
                print(e.diag.message_detail)


asyncio.run(main())
examples.output:
ForeignKeyViolation 23503 bookings_room_id_fkey
Key (room_id)=(99) is not present in table "rooms".
examples.explanation: The exception's class, `ForeignKeyViolation`, already says what happened, and `sqlstate` is the matching code, `23503`. `diag` holds the rest of what PostgreSQL sent: `constraint_name` names the exact rule, the foreign key PostgreSQL named for `bookings.room_id`, and `message_detail` says which value broke it. The detail is for your logs, not for the client, since it can include data the caller shouldn't see. In the repository, `except errors.ForeignKeyViolation` turns this into the domain's `room-not-found` problem, a 422.

recap:
- An ORM writes SQL for you and hides it, with N+1 queries as the classic cost, and this course writes SQL with psycopg instead.
- A pool keeps a few connections open, each request borrows one, and the pool opens at startup and closes at shutdown.
- Migrations are numbered SQL files a runner applies once each, in order, in transactions, and a file that ran is never edited.
- Values always travel as parameters, never inside the SQL text, and names like sort columns come from an allowlist in the code.
- The repository maps rows to domain types and turns no row into not found, which the service answers with a 404.
- Optional filters and keyset pages build the WHERE from fixed pieces, and ANY or a JOIN replaces N+1 queries.
- RETURNING gives back what a write stored, the row count tells whether it found the row, and SQLSTATEs map to 409 or 422.
